sections.html: All species of the Erethistes/Hara group grow to 4-5 cm and are excellent, peaceful and easy to care aquarium fishes.

In India live two species of moth catfishes, which are practically impossible to distinguish in living condition. They are nevertheless sometimes even assigned to two different genera: Hara and Erethistes. The difference between the two genera lies in the structure of the vertebral body, that is, of something invisible in the living animal; according to many ichthyologists, this is not enough to distinguish two genera, and then all moth catfishes would have to be assigned the generic name Erethistes, since this is older and has priority.

The difference between the species Hara hara ( = Erethistes hara) and Erethistes pusillus is only in the way the front of the pectoral fin spine is spined. In Erethistes pusillus the spines on the front of the pectoral fin spine are two pointed, in Hara hara ( = Erethistes hara) only one pointed. So you have to look at the pectoral fin spine in high magnification and back light to be sure which of the two species you have in front of you. But this does not mean that all specimens of the import belong to this species, because Hara hara ( = Erethistes hara) and Eretisthes pusillus occur in the same distribution area and are often caught and exported together.

In the trade no practicable method has been found to distinguish the two species with certainty, and therefore all moth catfishes of the Erethistes/Hara group imported from India (Bengal) are called Hara hara, with the exception of the well recognizable species Hara horai ( = Erethistes horai) and H. jerdoni ( = Erethistes jerdoni).
Asia: India, Ganges River basin, Assam. Type locality: Assam.
Occurs mainly in hill streams and muddy parts of rivers overgrown with vegetation.

A tank with a sandy bottom and rounded stones and pebbles with a good water flow, as befits an Asian hillstream setup. Good water quality is a must for this family. Keep the water temperature on the cool side of a tropical aquarium.
Prefers live foods such as bloodworm, grindal worm and daphnia.
Tank mates such as the zebra danio (Brachydanio rerio) and Asian fish of the same small size will make good tankmates.
The animals are called moth catfishes because their coloration and the broadly extending pectoral fins remind of night butterflies.

In Ferraris 2007, Erithistes has been moved back to its original placement in the Sisoridae family, where de Pinna placed it in 1996, along with Conta, Erethistoides, Hara and Pseudolaguvia.

Etymology: Erithistes, etymology not explained, presumably erethizon, porcupine, and -istes, adjectival suffix, i.e. porcupine-like, referring to strong and serrated dorsal and pectoral-fin spines. The species epithet pusillus means very small, presumably referring to size (4 cm SL).

IUCN Red List: Although the exact distribution of this species is not known, Erethistes pusillus appears to be relatively common wherever it occurs. Collection for the ornamental fish trade is currently at a level not projected to adversely affect the global population, so it is assessed as Least Concern, although future monitoring of harvest levels and identification of potential threats to its habitat is probably required (IUCN 2010).
